topic: All planets fit between Earth and Moon (Part 1, follow-CTA logged)
hook: All 7 planets fit between Earth and Moon

slides.title: The average gap
slides.body: The Moon sits about 384,400 km from Earth on average. Light crosses that gap in roughly 1.3 seconds.
slides.image_prompt: Earth and a small Moon floating far apart in black space, a thin glowing line stretching between them, cinematic lighting

slides.title: Line up the planets
slides.body: Put Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Venus, Mars and Mercury side by side. Together they span about 380,000 km.
slides.image_prompt: Seven planets lined up edge to edge in a row across dark space, Jupiter and Saturn largest, tiny Mercury at the end

slides.title: Only just
slides.body: That leaves about 4,400 km of space. Not even Mars, 6,779 km wide, would fit in the leftover gap.
slides.image_prompt: A small red planet squeezed into a narrow gap between a row of planets and the Moon, dramatic tight fit in space

slides.title: Not every night
slides.body: The Moon's orbit is an ellipse. At its closest, about 363,000 km away, the planets no longer fit.
slides.image_prompt: Elliptical orbit path drawn as a glowing ring around Earth, the Moon at its closest point, deep space background

cta: Part 2 tomorrow. Follow to catch it
caption:
Line up every other planet in our solar system, side by side, and they fill about 380,000 km. The average distance to the Moon is 384,400 km. So they fit, with roughly 4,400 km to spare.

The catch: the Moon's orbit is not a perfect circle. At its closest point it is about 363,000 km away, and then the planets no longer fit. Source: NASA planetary fact sheets. Part 2 tomorrow is about how big the Sun really is, so follow if you want it.

Be honest: did you think they would fit?
